findings.where: First screen, desktop and phone: the header lockup (the aqueduct mark with MMM INFRA, then 'Mark M. Moseley')
findings.fault: The mark comes first and is the larger graphic, and Mark's name follows it. The visitor reads the firm's logo before the man.
findings.who_objects: The founder. His personal-advisor test says Mark's name leads with the logo beside it. Here the logo leads, which drifts back toward 'the firm is the brand'.

findings.where: First screen, desktop: the overall composition (text panel on the left, portrait on the right, yellow address strip at the foot)
findings.fault: The hero is the stock split layout: words on the left and a head-and-shoulders photo on the right. Only the pale yellow strip and the hairline make it distinctive, so the first screen looks calm but generic.
findings.who_objects: The founder. He asked for 'alive, not boring' and rejected round 1's v5 for fine parts put together dully. A development-bank visitor may see a layout any consultancy could own.

findings.where: Whole page, beyond the hero: the article specimen and the end of the page
findings.fault: The article specimen shows no page header or footer. Nothing shows how an article page carries Mark's name, a way home or his address. The email appears only in the hero strip and nowhere at the foot of the page.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who arrives on an article from a LinkedIn post. With no name, home link or address on the page, they have no route to Mark. The founder also cannot judge the Read surface as a whole page.

findings.where: First screen, phone: the order of the headline, the yellow address strip and the 'I advise…' paragraph
findings.fault: On the phone the address strip comes before the supporting line, so the sentence saying what Mark does and for whom is cut off from the headline. It is left as an orphan below the yellow band, at the bottom of the frame. Desktop keeps the opposite, logical order.
findings.who_objects: A phone visitor gets asked to write before learning what Mark does, and may skip the line that tells them whether he fits their need.

findings.where: Article specimen, desktop: the Download row ('Streamlining the PPP Process…' with 'Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF')
findings.fault: The type, date and format line is pushed to the far right edge of the column, a long way from the title it describes. It reads as a separate item, not as the link's details.
findings.who_objects: A reader scanning for the lecture's date and format has to bridge the gap. With more than one PDF in a list, it would be unclear which details belong to which title.

findings.where: Article specimen: the Download link (parts p6 → #)
findings.fault: The only PDF link goes to '#'. It does nothing, and it shows no HTML gateway page or file size for the PDF.
findings.who_objects: A procurement reader who clicks to take the lecture gets nothing. The brief calls the article and the PDF list 'the product'.

findings.where: Motion sketch: 'Replay the entrance' (parts p7, a button)
findings.fault: A button that does something here is styled as a blue underlined link. It borrows the link colour and underline that the page keeps for navigation.
findings.who_objects: A visitor expects it to take them somewhere and is surprised when the line animates instead. The house's carriers rule keeps that look for links.

findings.where: Motion sketch, desktop and phone: the easing-curve box under 'Settled, unhurried, once.'
findings.fault: The curve's box is indented about 7 px from the column's left edge, which the heading and caption above and below share. It looks misplaced.
findings.who_objects: The founder, judging craft. A small misalignment on a page about precision reads as carelessness.

findings.where: Texture specimen: the framed box with the partial yellow bar
findings.fault: The yellow bar stops partway across an otherwise empty frame, with nothing on the right to explain where it ends. In the hero it ends at the photo's edge. Shown alone, the bar looks arbitrary.
findings.who_objects: The founder, reading the tile to decide whether the legal-pad idea holds. The specimen does not show how it really appears.

findings.where: First screen, desktop: the portrait's backdrop against the paper
findings.fault: The studio backdrop shows as a cool grey slab against the warm ivory paper. The palette note claims the photos are multiplied onto the paper 'so their light backdrops take the paper's warmth', but the render does not show this.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for the exact colours and shades to be right on the legal pad. The cool block breaks the single warm ground the direction promises.

findings.where: Article specimen: the title 'The World's Best…' and the closing paragraph's 'world's'
findings.fault: Straight typewriter apostrophes sit beside curly quotation marks in the same article ('chapter topics', the quoted question).
findings.who_objects: A careful reader at a bank or a ministry. Mixed quote marks undercut the 'legal journal' gravitas the direction aims for.

findings.where: First screen and the whole page: where Mark works
findings.fault: The page says what he does and for whom, but nowhere names the regions or countries of his work.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer screening against terms of reference that name a region. They cannot tell whether Mark has worked there.
